content: Argan oil is a natural oil extracted from the kernels of the argan tree, a species endemic to southwestern Morocco. This tree, a relic from the Tertiary age, is highly adapted to arid and challenging environmental conditions. Historically, the argan tree once covered much of North Africa but is now endangered and protected under UNESCO. Its deep root system plays a crucial role in preventing soil erosion and halting the northern expansion of the Sahara Desert. The tree thrives in semi-desert soils, and its habitat is part of the Arganeraie Biosphere Reserve, which spans over 2,560,000 hectares, bordered by the High Atlas and Anti-Atlas Mountains and extending to the Atlantic Ocean in the west. Argan oil is one of the rarest oils globally due to the limited and specific area in which the argan tree grows. The tree was first documented by the explorer Leo Africanus in 1510, and an early specimen was cultivated in Amsterdam and later by Lady Beaufort in England around 1711. Extraction of Argan Oil Traditional Method The traditional production of argan oil is a labor-intensive process, primarily carried out by women. The process begins with the removal of the soft pulp (known as afiasch in Berber), which is then sun-dried. The hard nuts are cracked manually between two stones to extract the seeds. These seeds are gently roasted, a step that imparts the oil's characteristic nutty flavor. The roasted seeds are ground into a dough using a stone rotary quern, with a small amount of water added. The resulting paste is hand-squeezed to extract the oil. The leftover paste, called amlou, remains rich in oil. Oil produced using this method has a shelf life of 3–6 months and is typically made as needed from stored kernels, which can remain viable for up to 20 years if unopened. Press-Extraction For commercial purposes, mechanical presses are increasingly used to extract argan oil. This method eliminates the need to mix the dough with water, allowing the dough to be pressed directly. The process yields approximately 43% oil from the kernels and takes only about two hours to produce one liter of oil. The oil extracted this way has a longer shelf life of 12–18 months. Solvent-Extraction In industrial or laboratory settings, argan oil can be extracted using volatile lipophilic solvents. After the solvent is evaporated and the process is repeated one or two times, the oil yield is between 50–55%. However, this method produces oil with inferior organoleptic properties compared to traditional or press-extracted oil. As a result, solvent-extracted oil is reserved exclusively for cosmetic applications. Properties and Uses of Argan Oil Argan oil is exceptionally rich in natural tocopherols (vitamin E), phenols, phenolic acids, carotenes, squalene, and essential fatty acids, with 80% of its fatty acids being unsaturated. Depending on the extraction method, it is more resistant to oxidation than olive oil. Culinary uses of argan oil include dipping bread, drizzling over couscous, and dressing salads. The residue from traditional oil extraction, amlou, is a thick, chocolate-colored paste that is sweetened and served as a bread dip, often compared in flavor to peanut butter. Unroasted argan oil has been traditionally used to treat skin diseases and is now widely utilized in the cosmetics industry. Research has shown promising results for its potential in treating psoriasis. Medicinal Uses Argan oil has been studied for its therapeutic properties, particularly in the treatment of psoriasis, with encouraging outcomes. It is also increasingly sought after by cosmetics companies for its skin-nourishing benefits. Commercial Availability Argan oil is sold in Morocco as both a luxury item and a more affordable product in ordinary shops and supermarkets. Historically difficult to find outside Morocco, it gained popularity in Europe and North America as a fashionable food item around 2001–2002. It is now widely available in specialty stores and some supermarkets, with prices reflecting its status as a premium product, often marketed as a superfood. Myths and Misconceptions Goats are known to consume the pulp of argan fruits and often climb the trees to access them. While the goats digest the pulp, they excrete the undigested seeds in their feces. These seeds, with their softened shells, are sometimes used to produce oil for non-culinary purposes. However, the myth that all argan oil is derived this way is unfounded. Occasionally, unscrupulous traders have sold such non-food grade oil to unsuspecting tourists. The distinct foul aroma of oil produced from goat-digested seeds makes it easy to differentiate from high-quality, food-grade argan oil, which has a rich, walnut-like flavor.
